Newly settled spat of the Great scallop Pecten maximus emerge from the egg capsule with a shell height of just 0.008 cm [Lb = 0.008 cm], a minute dimension that marks the beginning of a complex life history. This initial size corresponds to an extremely low dry weight of 0.000000104 grams , reflecting the limited maternal investment per zygote. The transition from a free-swimming veliger larva to a benthic juvenile is contingent upon successful metamorphosis, a critical developmental bottleneck during which the larval velum is resorbed and the gill rudiments form. At metamorphosis, individuals exhibit a shell height of 0.024 cm  and carry a dry weight of only 0.000003 grams . The duration of the planktonic larval phase, measured from the moment of hatching, is approximately 25 days from the moment of hatching  when the water temperature is maintained at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], a thermal regime typical of the species' native coastal waters. This relatively brief pelagic period, characteristic of many pectinids, limits the potential for long-distance dispersal and contributes to the genetic structure observed among local populations.

Juvenile scallops, having passed through metamorphic climax, begin a period of rapid somatic growth that eventually culminates in the attainment of adult size. Under favorable conditions, the maximum recorded shell height for a fully grown individual is 12.0 cm [Li = 12.0 cm], a dimension typical of large, reproductively active specimens from productive fishing grounds. This asymptotic shell length corresponds to an ultimate dry weight of 20 grams , a value derived from length-weight regressions that exhibit a high coefficient of determination across multiple sampled cohorts. The life history strategy of Pecten maximus is characterized by a notable longevity; field records and tag-recapture studies indicate that the oldest documented individuals can live for 20 years [am = 20 years] when residing in waters that average 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This extended lifespan, unusual among bivalves of similar body size, allows for multiple reproductive seasons and contributes to the species' resilience under moderate fishing pressure, as older individuals buffer the population against years of poor recruitment.

Sexual maturation in the Great scallop is a gradual process that begins once the animal reaches a distinct size threshold rather than a fixed age. The onset of puberty, defined by the first appearance of gonadal tissue and active gametogenesis, occurs when the shell height is approximately 4.0 cm [Lp = approximately 4.0 cm]. At this point, the corresponding dry weight of the animal is about 1 gram , a value obtained from the same length-weight regression used for adult mass estimates. The time elapsed from hatching to the initiation of gonadal activity is approximately 365 days from hatching [tp = approximately 365 days from hatching] under standard thermal conditions of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This one-year lag between settlement and the first signs of reproductive development is a common feature of pectinid life histories in temperate waters, allowing juveniles to channel resources into shell and somatic growth before diverting energy toward gamete production. Once mature, individuals spawn repeatedly over successive seasons, contributing to a protracted annual reproductive period that may last several months.

Reproductive output in Pecten maximus is strongly modulated by water temperature, with peak fecundity observed under optimal thermal conditions. At a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], a single large female can produce as many as 57,534 eggs per day [Ri = 57,534 eggs per day], a remarkable rate of gamete release sustained over the spawning peak. This enormous daily fecundity, among the highest recorded for any scallop species, reflects the energetic investment necessary to offset high larval mortality in the plankton. The age at which this maximum reproductive rate is typically achieved coincides with the attainment of full adult size, as older and larger individuals possess greater gonad volume and a more extensive digestive gland capable of supporting elevated metabolic demands. Temperature plays a dual role in this process: it governs the rate of gametogenesis and also dictates the timing of spawning events, which often follow rapid thermal fluctuations in the spring or autumn. The reproductive strategy is thus closely attuned to local oceanographic conditions, with populations adjusting their spawning intensity in response to thermal cues.

The earliest life stages of the Great scallop are particularly sensitive to thermal conditions, with temperature exerting a strong influence on both developmental rate and hatching success. Embryonated eggs incubated at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] hatch after just 2 days [ab = just 2 days], a rapid embryonic development that reduces the window of vulnerability to benthic predators and pathogens. This temperature-dependent acceleration of early ontogeny is typical of marine bivalves, though the exact rate varies among populations adapted to local thermal regimes. The fecundation event itself occurs via external fertilisation following the simultaneous release of gametes into the water column, a process facilitated by chemical cues and hydrodynamic mixing during spawning aggregations. Shortly after hatching, the trochophore larva develops into a free-swimming veliger, which relies on cilia-driven feeding to acquire phytoplankton from the water column. The subsequent timing of metamorphosis, at roughly 25 days post-hatching  under stable 13 °C [T = 13 °C] conditions, represents a critical juncture where successful settlement on suitable substrate determines the survival trajectory of the cohort.
